Thrush (oral yeast infection): White patches on the baby's tongue or inside the cheeks that don't wipe off may be thrush; it can also affect a breastfeeding mother's nipples.
Thrush is caused by overgrowth of a yeast that normally lives in the mouth.
Milk residue wipes off easily; thrush patches don't, and trying to wipe them may leave redness.
A breastfeeding mother may have burning, itching and a shiny pink look on the nipple.
Wash and boil dummies, teats and breast pump parts after every use.
If treatment is needed, baby and breastfeeding mother are treated together; use the medicine for as long as the doctor advises.
Don't try to scrape off the patches.
If the baby refuses feeds or has fewer wet nappies.
If the patches don't clear within 1 week or keep coming back.
If there's a stubborn nappy rash with red dots at the edges.
Umbilical and inguinal hernia
A bulge at the belly button is common in babies and most close by themselves; a swelling in the groin should be seen by a doctor.
An umbilical hernia is a soft bulge that shows more when crying; most close on their own by age 1–4.
An inguinal hernia appears as a swelling that comes and goes in the groin, or in the scrotum in boys, and usually needs surgical repair.
Inguinal hernia is more common in premature babies.
Don't tie tape, a coin or a belt on the belly button; it doesn't work and can harm the skin.
Take a photo of the swelling and show it to the doctor at the check-up.
If you notice a swelling in the groin, see a doctor soon.
If the swelling becomes hard, red or painful and won't go back in: go to A&E immediately.
If the hernia comes with vomiting, a swollen tummy and fussiness: go to A&E immediately.
Baby poo: colour and frequency
The colour and frequency of baby poo vary a lot with feeding; apart from a few colours, most differences are normal.
The dark green-black poo of the first days (meconium) turns yellow within a few days.
In breastfed babies yellow, soft, seedy poo is normal; it may come several times a day or once every few days.
In formula-fed babies poo may be darker and firmer.
Note any sudden change in colour or frequency in the journal.
If you see a worrying colour, take a photo of the nappy.
Keep track of wet nappies; it's a good sign of adequate feeding.
White, grey or very pale poo: see a doctor the same day.
Blood in the poo, or black tar-like poo (after the meconium period): see a doctor the same day.
Frequent watery poo with few wet nappies, listlessness or fever.
Undescended testicle
In some baby boys one or both testicles may not have come down into the scrotum; most come down by themselves in the first months.
It is more common in babies born prematurely.
If the testicle hasn't come down in the first 6 months, it usually won't by itself and needs treatment.
Treatment is usually a small operation done between 6 and 18 months.
Ask for the testicles to be checked at vaccination and check-up visits.
Looking at the scrotum when the baby is relaxed in a warm bath makes checking easier.
A testicle still not felt in the scrotum at 6 months.
Sudden swelling, redness and severe pain in the scrotum: go to A&E immediately.
Stuttering and fluency
Word repetitions are common between ages 2 and 5 and are temporary in most children.
Repeating syllables or words can be normal while language develops rapidly.
Stretching sounds, blocks, facial tension and avoiding speaking can be signs of persistent stuttering.
A family history of stuttering increases the risk.
Listen patiently; don't finish their sentence or say “speak slowly”.
Set an example by speaking slowly and calmly yourself.
Set aside a few unhurried minutes of one-to-one chat every day.
If the blocks last longer than 6 months or are increasing.
If the child avoids speaking, feels ashamed or shows facial tension.
If stuttering continues after age 5: see a speech and language therapist.
Night terrors and nightmares
In a night terror the child may look awake but is asleep; in a nightmare they wake up and remember the dream.
Night terrors usually happen in the first hours of sleep; the child screams and sweats but doesn't remember in the morning.
Nightmares happen in the second half of the night; the child wakes up scared and wants comfort.
Tiredness, irregular sleep and stress can increase both.
During a night terror don't try to wake the child; stay nearby so they don't fall or bump into things.
After a nightmare, hug, soothe and stay in the room.
Keep a regular bedtime and a calm routine; avoid scary content before bed.
If episodes are very frequent or cause daytime tiredness.
If a seizure is suspected (jerking, wetting, confusion in the morning).
If you notice snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep.
Thumb and dummy sucking habit
Thumb sucking is natural in infancy; most children stop by themselves at 2–4 years.
The sucking reflex soothes the baby.
Heavy sucking that continues after permanent teeth start coming in can affect tooth alignment.
Shaming and punishment usually make the habit worse.
Notice when sucking increases (tiredness, boredom, anxiety).
Offer other ways to calm down, such as games that keep the hands busy and cuddles.
Plan a gradual end to the dummy around age 2–3.
If it continues intensely after age 4: talk to a dentist.
If there's a sore, callus or infection on the finger.
Biting, hitting and aggressive behaviour
Young children may bite or hit when they can't yet express feelings in words.
It's common between ages 1 and 3 and mostly temporary.
Tiredness, hunger, crowds and frustration can be triggers.
A calm, consistent response from adults helps the behaviour fade.
Say it calmly and briefly: “Biting hurts, I won't let you.”
